statement.p: For each of the following, decide if the given vector field is a gradient of a function f. If so, give find the function f and enter it as your answer; if not, enter the word none for your answer and be sure that you are able to explain why this is the case.
(c) [ 8 x y ]\,\vec i + [ 4 x^2 ]\,\vec j: f =

static.solution:
(a) No. To see this, suppose we integrate \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} to find f. This gives f(x,y) = 2 x^2\cos(y^2) + C(y), so that, differentiating again, we would have to have \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = -4 x^2 y\sin(y^2) + C'(y). For no choice of C can we make this work, so there is no such function f.
(b) Yes. We can find f by integrating \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} to find f. This gives f(x,y) = 4 x^2 + C(y), so that, differentiating again, we have \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 4 x^2 + C'(y). Thus we may take f(x,y) = 4x^{2}+3y^{2}+K.
(c) Yes. We can find f by integrating \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} to find f. This gives f(x,y) = 4 x^2 y + C(y), so that, differentiating again, we have \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 4 x^2 + C'(y). Thus we may take f(x,y) = 4x^{2}y+K.
(d) Yes. We can find f by integrating \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} to find f. This gives f(x,y) = 8 x\cos(x^2 + 4y^2) + C(x), so that, differentiating again, we have \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 8 \cos(x^2 + 4y^2) - 16\sin(x^2 + 4y^2) + C'(x). Thus we may take f(x,y) = 8x\cos\mathopen{}\left(x^{2}+4y^{2}\right)+K.
